Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
Assume: I have an acting Toreador (who is very good at dodging)
in combat with a blocking Brujah (who is very good at hurting)

in a round of combat, my Tor (suspecting large damage) Dodges.
the Brutejah pouts and simply announces a hand strike.

My Tor doesn't play a card to gain an additional strike.
The Brute, however, Blurs for two more strikes.

Q: can my Timid Tor now play Blur to gain additional strikes?
(And use those to dodge two more times?)

That is: is gaining additional strikes like blocking (once passed,
you can't choose to later), or is it like Pressing/Maneuvering
and stealth/intercept (playable in response to the opposing Minion's
activity)?

It is like blocking, IMHO - since you either do or you don't,
and since presses/maneuver/intercept-stealth can be gained an
arbitrary number of times until one minion "wins".

Tom? Care to give the official stance on this?
--
L. Scott Johnson (sjoh...@math.scarolina.edu) | These opinions are mine and
Graphics Specialist and Jyhad Rulemonger. | are subject to card text.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Joseph Cochran <js...@discus.ise.vt.edu> wrote:
>>If the acting minion plays a dodge, the blocking minion is perfectly free
>>to respond with a strike. That strike simply won't do anything to the
>>dodging minion (well, except that combat ends works normally).
> I thought that you had said that Dodge took effect immediately
>like CE did. What did you actually mean?

Dodge automatically neutralizes the other strike, even if it's done at
first strike, so yes it basically takes effect immediately. But it's always
legal to play a strike that you know is going to fail, e.g. playing Undead
Strength when the round is at range.

>Strength when the round is at range.
>

I think (as we all know) the point Joe Cochran was trying to make was
that even though Dodge and Combat Ends "basically take effect immediately"
they really take effect during strike resolution - just like every other
strike. You say that this is the case for Dodge - cancelling the
opposing offensive strike (even a first strike), but you refuse to clear
the fog from the Combat Ends ruling. It could easily follow the rules
of logic and consistency by saying that the Combat Ends takes effect during
the strike resolution - cancelling the opposing offensive strike (even a
first strike). You cannot "play a strike that you know is going to fail" -
which you say you can always do, because the DT has corrupted the system
after someone mis-read too much into the word "immediately" in the rulebook.
What's wrong with playing it the way the rules are written?

If you keep clinging to this false ruling, then more and more silly, circular
conversations (like the one between me and Joe that prompted your response)
will pop up - because the ruling isn't solidly based.
It will fall eventually - may as well be sooner.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
L. Scott Johnson <lsc...@crl.com> wrote:

>I think (as we all know) the point Joe Cochran was trying to make was
>that even though Dodge and Combat Ends "basically take effect immediately"
>they really take effect during strike resolution - just like every other

>strike...

Look, I realize everyone here wants to shoehorn dodge and combat ends into
the same process that all other strikes follow, but they don't. "Combat ends"
ends the combat *immediately*, as the strike is played, before anything else
can happen. The effects of Dodge also kick in immediately. If you really
hate this rule, you are free to play with a house rule, but this *is* how the
strikes are officially supposed to work, and how they were designed to work.
Not all strikes are created equally.

>You cannot "play a strike that you know is going to fail" -
>which you say you can always do, because the DT has corrupted the system
>after someone mis-read too much into the word "immediately" in the rulebook.
>What's wrong with playing it the way the rules are written?

Where in the rulebook does it say that you can't play a strike you know is
going to fail? That you can't play Undead Strength when the combat is at
range? That you can't use a weapon that is being Shattered with first strike?
That you can't use Theft of Vitae on an empty vampire? Everyone is complaining
that an acting minion playing combat ends means the blocking minion can't
burn a card on a strike, yet you seem to have pulled this rule out of a hat.

>If you keep clinging to this false ruling, then more and more silly, circular
>conversations (like the one between me and Joe that prompted your response)
>will pop up - because the ruling isn't solidly based.

The fact that you don't like the rule does not make it inconsistent. These
two strikes are simply different from all of the others. In fact, dodging
isn't really a strike at all (see section 15.1, "Choose Strike").

Messages.Author: Thomas Doehne
Messages.Body:
In article <3pu47p$n...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU> aa...@cats.ucsc.edu
(Thomas R Wylie) writes:

>L. Scott Johnson <lsc...@crl.com> wrote:

[CE Official Line deleted]

>>Nowhere does the rulesbook say "when played" - it describes all of the strike
>>effects as how they resolve.

>"Considered a strike, this ends combat immediately (before any damage is
>dealt or any strike's effects take place)." Corrected rules, page 8. What
>else could that be supposed to mean?

Lessee, maybe it means exactly what it seems to mean -- that none of
the strikes played do any damage, and that no other strikes have
any effect. It certainly *doesn't* say that no other strikes
can be played, only that other strikes have no effect. Also, that
other things, like retainers, do no damage. Basically, the quote
seems to say that CE is the first thing that happens during
resolution.

The DT may want CE to prevent the playing of any other strikes, but
the rules sure don't read that way. If you were hoping this quote
would convince anyone, you're out of luck -- it's convinced me that,
just as Scott said, the official ruling on CE is plucked from
very thin air.

--
